```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE)
```

A fitted model can be wrong in ways its own estimates do not show. Subjects
may differ in a parameter the model holds fixed; a parameter may depend on a
covariate that was never put in the model; the dynamics may depend on where the
process is. `ctScoreTest()` asks of one fitted model, without refitting it,
whether any of these relaxations would fit better, and if so where:

* **heterogeneity**: does a parameter differ between subjects, so that it
  should be individually varying?
* **covariates**: does a parameter depend on a subject-level covariate the
  model does not contain -- including the size of a random effect, not only
  its mean?
* **state dependence**: does a drift coefficient change with the level of a
  latent state, so that the dynamics are nonlinear?

Each is a score (Lagrange multiplier) test: the slope of the log likelihood,
at the fitted model, in the direction of the relaxation. It needs a few
evaluations of the fitted model's gradient rather than a new fit per
candidate, so any number of candidates can be screened after one fit, and each
test also says roughly how large the relaxation would be. The tests are
screens: they point at what to relax, and the refit says how much it matters.

The three examples below each generate data with one thing the fitted model
lacks, fit the model without it, ask `ctScoreTest()`, and then refit with what
it found. The sections after them add a fourth family of tests (cells the
model fixes at zero), the posterior predictive checks as tests
(`ctFitAdequacy()`), and a search that combines the two and does the
refitting itself (`ctModelImprove()`).

```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
set.seed(3)
```

## The process

Two latent processes, each measured by one indicator, observed 30 times at
irregular intervals for 150 subjects. `eta1` regulates towards its baseline at
rate 0.6, `eta2` at 0.4, and `eta1` pushes `eta2` up (a cross effect of 0.25).
Each subject has their own measurement intercepts. The generating model is
written once, and each example changes one cell of it.

```{r generator}
generator <- function(DRIFT, MANIFESTMEANS = c("mm1|param|TRUE|1", "mm2|param|TRUE|1"),
  TIpredNames = NULL) {
  ctModel(type = "ct", silent = TRUE,
    manifestNames = c("Y1", "Y2"), latentNames = c("eta1", "eta2"),
    LAMBDA = diag(2), DRIFT = DRIFT, CINT = matrix(0, 2, 1),
    DIFFUSION = matrix(c(0.8, 0, 0, 0.6), 2, 2), MANIFESTVAR = diag(0.5, 2),
    MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(MANIFESTMEANS, 2, 1),
    T0MEANS = matrix(0, 2, 1), T0VAR = diag(1, 2), TIpredNames = TIpredNames)
}
```

The model fitted in every example is ctsem's default for two latents with one
indicator each: every drift, diffusion and measurement error parameter free
and shared by all subjects, and individually varying measurement intercepts
and initial states.

```{r model}
model <- ctModel(type = "ct", silent = TRUE,
  manifestNames = c("Y1", "Y2"), latentNames = c("eta1", "eta2"),
  LAMBDA = diag(2))
```

## 1. Subjects who differ in a parameter

Here the subjects differ in how quickly `eta1` regulates: the drift
`DRIFT[1,1]` varies between subjects around -0.6, with a standard deviation of
about 0.25.

```{r het-generate}
gen1 <- generator(DRIFT = matrix(c("drift11|-log1p_exp(-param)|TRUE|0.6", 0.25,
  0, -0.4), 2, 2))
d1 <- ctGenerate(gen1, n = 150, Tpoints = 30, dtmean = 1, logdtsd = 0.5,
  backend = "julia", popmeans = c(drift11 = -0.6, mm1 = 0, mm2 = 0))
truedrift <- attr(d1, "subjectpars")$drift11
c(mean = mean(truedrift), sd = sd(truedrift))
d1 <- data.frame(d1)
```

The default model shares one drift among all subjects.

```{r het-fit}
fit1 <- ctFit(d1, model, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
st1 <- ctScoreTest(fit1, tests = "heterogeneity")
st1
```

Each row tests whether that parameter's variance over subjects is zero; the
test is one sided, since a variance cannot be negative. The drift of `eta1` is
flagged, and so is its diffusion. That is expected rather than a second
finding: a subject whose process regulates more slowly also varies more, so
the subjects disagree about the diffusion too. The test says that the subjects
differ, and roughly where; it cannot always say which of two related
parameters is the source. The way to find out is to relax the strongest
candidate and test again.

```{r het-refit}
model1b <- model
model1b$pars$indvarying[model1b$pars$param %in% "drift_eta1"] <- TRUE
fit1b <- ctFit(d1, model1b, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
c(loglik_without = fit1$estimate$loglik, loglik_with = fit1b$estimate$loglik)
ctScoreTest(fit1b, tests = "heterogeneity")
```

With the drift free to vary the log likelihood rises by about 12, and
nothing else stands out: the diffusion's signal was the drift's. (A drift that
varies between subjects enters the filter nonlinearly, so `ctFit()` chose the
Laplace route for the refit; the tests work on either.)

## 2. A covariate the model does not contain

Now each subject has an `age` (standardised), and age matters twice: older
subjects have a higher intercept on `Y1`, and in older subjects `eta1` pushes
`eta2` harder (the cross effect `DRIFT[2,1]` rises by 0.3 per standard
deviation of age). A second covariate, `w`, is unrelated to anything.

```{r cov-generate}
gen2 <- generator(DRIFT = matrix(c(-0.6, "drift21||||age=0.3", 0, -0.4), 2, 2),
  MANIFESTMEANS = c("mm1|param|TRUE|1|age=0.6", "mm2|param|TRUE|1"),
  TIpredNames = c("age", "w"))
d2 <- data.frame(ctGenerate(gen2, n = 150, Tpoints = 30, dtmean = 1,
  logdtsd = 0.5, backend = "julia", popmeans = c(drift21 = 0.25, mm1 = 0, mm2 = 0)))
covariates <- unique(d2[, c("id", "age", "w")])
head(covariates)
```

The model is fitted without either covariate, and the covariates are handed to
`ctScoreTest()` afterwards, one row per subject.

```{r cov-fit}
fit2 <- ctFit(d2[, c("id", "time", "Y1", "Y2")], model, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
st2 <- ctScoreTest(fit2, covariates = covariates, tests = "covariates")
st2
```

For each covariate, the joint test asks whether it matters anywhere; then each
parameter's row gives the effect a refit with that covariate would be expected
to estimate, per unit of the covariate. `age` is found, on the intercept of
`Y1` and on the cross effect, at about the sizes it was generated with; `w` is
not. Two things make that attribution work. The effects are estimated jointly,
so a covariate that moves one parameter is not read off another that happens
to be correlated with it. And they are estimated with the fitted model's
parameters held where the fit left them: the model without `age` has already
absorbed some of its effect -- the intercepts' standard deviation has grown to
take in the age differences -- and an estimate that lets those parameters move
too extrapolates the model's curvature across that whole change.

The tests also cover the random effects' standard deviations (the `popsd_`
rows): whether subjects differ more at some ages than others.

The refit puts `age` into the model as a time independent predictor, with
effects on every parameter:

```{r cov-refit}
model2b <- ctModel(type = "ct", silent = TRUE,
  manifestNames = c("Y1", "Y2"), latentNames = c("eta1", "eta2"),
  LAMBDA = diag(2), TIpredNames = "age")
fit2b <- ctFit(d2, model2b, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
effects <- summary(fit2b)$tipreds
effects[grepl("mm_Y1|drift_eta2_eta1", rownames(effects)), ]
```

## 3. Dynamics that depend on the state

Last, `eta2` moderates how `eta1` regulates: when `eta2` is high, `eta1`
returns to baseline more slowly. The drift of `eta1` is
`-0.6 + 0.3 * tanh(eta2)`, so it ranges between -0.9 and -0.3, and near
`eta2 = 0` it rises by about 0.3 per unit of `eta2`.

```{r sdep-generate}
gen3 <- generator(DRIFT = matrix(c("-0.6 + 0.3 * tanh(eta2)", 0.25, 0, -0.4), 2, 2))
d3 <- data.frame(ctGenerate(gen3, n = 150, Tpoints = 30, dtmean = 1,
  logdtsd = 0.5, backend = "julia", popmeans = c(mm1 = 0, mm2 = 0)))
```

The fitted model is linear: each drift coefficient is a constant.

```{r sdep-fit}
fit3 <- ctFit(d3, model, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
st3 <- ctScoreTest(fit3, tests = "statedependence")
st3
```

Each term is one drift coefficient varying linearly with one state. The term
`eta1*eta2` in the equation of `eta1` stands out: either the drift of `eta1`
changes with `eta2` -- which is what generated the data -- or the effect of
`eta2` on `eta1` changes with `eta1`. At this order the two are the same term,
so the table names both, and which reading to fit is a substantive choice. The
estimate is the change in the drift coefficient per unit of the state. Writing
the dependence into the model:

```{r sdep-refit}
model3b <- ctModel(type = "ct", silent = TRUE,
  manifestNames = c("Y1", "Y2"), latentNames = c("eta1", "eta2"),
  LAMBDA = diag(2),
  DRIFT = matrix(c("dr11 + dstate * eta2", "dr21", "dr12", "dr22"), 2, 2),
  PARS = c("dr11|-log1p_exp(-param)", "dstate"))
fit3b <- ctFit(d3, model3b, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
c(loglik_without = fit3$estimate$loglik, loglik_with = fit3b$estimate$loglik)
summary(fit3b)$popmeans[c("dr11", "dstate"), ]
```

The refit's `dstate` is a little smaller than the one-step estimate: the
generating `tanh` flattens away from zero, and a term linear in `eta2`
averages over its whole range. The first screen also flagged a second, weaker
term, `eta1*eta1` in the equation of `eta2`. That one was an echo -- the misfit
in `eta1`'s dynamics reaches `eta2` through the cross effect -- and testing the
refitted model shows nothing left:

```{r sdep-retest}
ctScoreTest(fit3b, tests = "statedependence")
```

The term already in the model now has no score left at all, and no other
term stands out.

The test works because the filter evaluates each candidate term at the state
it predicts from earlier observations. A weight that has not seen the
observation being scored keeps that observation's contribution to the score at
mean zero when the model is right. Using smoothed or updated state estimates
as covariates instead -- regressing something on the estimated states after
the fit -- does not have that property, and rejects correct models: in
simulation, nearly always.

## Everything at once

By default `ctScoreTest()` runs every family: the three above (covariates when
given) and a fourth, the cells the model fixes at zero -- here the measurement
error covariance and the cross loadings -- each tested as though freed. On the
last dataset:

```{r all}
ctScoreTest(fit3)
```

The state dependence stands out. The heterogeneity tests stay quiet here, but
they need not: a drift that changes with the state can also look, subject by
subject, like a drift that differs between subjects, and in simulations a
missing nonlinearity did move them. A badly misspecified model can light up
several tests at once, so read them as a map: relax what stands out most,
refit, and test again.

## Do the model's predictions look like the data?

The usual check of a dynamic model compares the data with data the fitted
model generates: the autocorrelations and cross-correlations (ACF and CCF),
how much subjects differ from each other, and so on. `ctFitAdequacy()` makes
those comparisons numbers with p-values, in families aimed at different
departures. Four compare statistics of the data with the same statistics of
generated data: the lagged correlations; the spread over subjects of each
subject's own mean, standard deviation and lag-one correlations; whether
change depends on level nonlinearly; and, given covariates, whether subjects'
statistics depend on them. Four more need no generated data, because they
work on the one-step-ahead prediction errors, which under the model are
independent and standard normal however the observations are spaced: whether
those errors are white (the residual ACF and CCF), whether they are normal,
whether some subjects are fitted worse than the model allows, and whether an
error or its size depends, in any form, on what came before it -- the
predicted states, the previous errors, the time since the last observation.
Each variable's error is taken given the others observed at the same time,
so a result names a variable.

On the second example's fit, which lacks `age`, the checks fail, through the
subjects' spread and their relation to age:

```{r adequacy-cov}
ctFitAdequacy(fit2, covariates = covariates)
```

On the linear fit to the state-dependent data:

```{r adequacy}
ctFitAdequacy(fit3)
```

Every family passes, though this model is missing the state dependence the
score test found at p = 5e-6. A moderated drift, averaged over the data,
still decays much like a single exponential, and summary statistics are
coarse instruments for a departure the likelihood sees directly. The lagged
correlations are the bluntest: they are close to what the fit was chosen to
reproduce, so they sit near the model's whatever else is wrong. The checks
are worth having: they catch what lies outside every score test's reach,
such as a process of the wrong order or errors with heavy tails. But passing
them is necessary rather than sufficient, which is why the next section
screens with the score tests and stops on the checks.

## Automating the search

`ctModelImprove()` puts the tests into a loop. It screens the fit, refits with
the most strongly indicated relaxations one at a time (warm started from the
current estimates), and keeps the best if the refit's likelihood confirms it.
It repeats until nothing more is indicated, then checks the model with
`ctFitAdequacy()`. If a check fails, it tries structural changes the score
tests cannot reach, such as making a process second order
(`ctModelHigherOrder()`) or models you supply. Finally it tries dropping each
change it kept, in case a later one made it redundant.

Here the data contain two of the departures above at once: `age` acts on the
intercept of `Y1` and on the cross effect, `eta2` moderates how `eta1`
regulates, and `w` is unrelated.

```{r improve-generate}
gen4 <- generator(DRIFT = matrix(c("-0.6 + 0.3 * tanh(eta2)", "drift21||||age=0.3",
  0, -0.4), 2, 2),
  MANIFESTMEANS = c("mm1|param|TRUE|1|age=0.6", "mm2|param|TRUE|1"),
  TIpredNames = c("age", "w"))
d4 <- data.frame(ctGenerate(gen4, n = 150, Tpoints = 30, dtmean = 1,
  logdtsd = 0.5, backend = "julia", popmeans = c(drift21 = 0.25, mm1 = 0, mm2 = 0)))
fit4 <- ctFit(d4[, c("id", "time", "Y1", "Y2")], model, backend = "julia", cores = 2)
```

```{r improve}
imp <- ctModelImprove(fit4, covariates = unique(d4[, c("id", "age", "w")]))
imp
```

Each round shows what was tried, the score test that proposed it, and what
the refit's likelihood said. The first round kept `age`, with effects on the
cross effect, the intercept of `Y1` and the initial level of `eta1`; it also
tried a random effect on the
cross effect, which the score tests had flagged because subjects of different
ages differ in it -- a covariate that explains the variation beats a random
effect that only describes it. The second round kept the moderation. Then
nothing more was indicated, every adequacy check passed, and trying each kept
change out again showed both were still needed. The effects found are near
those that generated the data (0.3 on the cross effect, 0.6 on the intercept
of `Y1`). The effect on the initial level of `eta1` was not generated: it is
small, and only just significant -- a search that decides at `alpha = 0.05`
keeps such things about one time in twenty, and `alpha = 0.01` is the
stricter choice.

The final fit is an ordinary fit:

```{r improve-final}
s <- summary(imp$fit)
s$tipreds
s$popmeans[grepl("^sdep", rownames(s$popmeans)), ]
```

The model was chosen by the data it is fitted to, so its standard errors and
tests are too optimistic about the structure the search added. Treat that
structure as a hypothesis: confirm it on other data, or hold out some
subjects from the search for that purpose.

## How the tests work, briefly

* The scores are those of the objective the model was fitted with, so they
  integrate over random effects exactly as the fit did. A covariate's effect
  adds to a parameter's raw value, so its score is the covariate times each
  subject's score in that parameter -- any number of covariates costs a few
  matrix products after one set of per-subject scores and Hessians.
* A random effect's variance has, at zero, the score
  $\frac{1}{2}\sum_i (s_{ij}^2 + H_{i,jj})$: the information matrix test in that
  parameter, which is the score test for neglected heterogeneity.
* State dependence is tested on the fitted model extended with the drift terms
  at zero, which reproduces the fit exactly there.
* The fitted model's curvature projects the fitted parameters out of each test
  and sizes the one-step estimates; each test's variance is the spread of the
  subjects' contributions, and its p-value comes from resampling subjects. That
  keeps a test valid when the model is wrong in some other way -- the case a
  screen is for -- where a variance from the model's own curvature would make
  unrelated tests reject too.

The tests need subjects as independent units, so a model with levels above the
subject can be tested for state dependence only. See `?ctScoreTest` for the
details.
